newsitem.title: ALBANIA: International force in Albania has first casualty.
newsitem.headline: International force in Albania has first casualty.

text.p: A multi-national security force in Albania suffered its first casualty when a Turkish soldier guarding the international airport was hit in the hand by a stray bullet, a military spokesman said on Friday.

Lieutenant Colonel Paolo Bianchi said the injured man was among 700 heavily armed Italian and Turkish soldiers who have taken control of Rinas airport, 25 kms (15 miles) outside the capital of Tirana, over the past week.

With the airport secure, six civilian flights are now arriving daily, bringing in businessmen, homebound Albanians and journalists, as well as up to 22 military flights transporting food and medical supplies for the needy.
"The soldier was protecting the perimeter fence of the airport when he was hit by a bullet, possibly a falling bullet, on Wednesday. It appears to have been accidental," Bianchi told Reuters.
"He was not seriously hurt but he is in the military hospital. This was our first casualty."
Many of the 300 plus deaths and 700 injuries in Albania over the past two months have been caused by stray bullets.

Thousands of Albanians, including children, are carrying guns after raiding state arsenals in the chaos that prevailed after five get-rich-quick "pyramid" schemes, in which many people had invested their life savings, collapsed in January.

As protestors took to the streets, blaming President Sali Berisha for the loss of their money, the army disintegrated and police fled, leaving state buildings unguarded. Services, including food and medical distibution, ground to a halt.

Colonel Alissandro Puzzilli, from Italy's 187th regiment, said the 6,000-strong United Nations- approved security force now flooding into Albania had helped restore normalcy, even though anti-Berisha rebels still control much of the south.
Soldiers are on guard 24 hours a day at Rinas, where 11 armed helicopters are on standby.
"The helicopter group is here to secure the airport, for reconnaissance, for escorts and protection," Puzzilli told journalists at the troops' airport base.
"They are not supposed to attack anyone. We have brought them because they are very good aircraft. They can fly in any weather conditions."
Puzzilli said the airport may soon allow flights around-the-clock despite the 8 pm - 6am curfew that rules across the rest of the small Balkan country.
"So far we have not had any problems and the situation here at the airport is good," he said.
"We have established good relations with local authorities and we are moving around, showing the flag, so people realise we're here to help and to secure the internationally supplied aid for them."
